Params: The wind snapped the ship's flag taut.
The sea churned and hurled itself against the hull, each wave shattering into a burst of white spray.
The vessel rolled without mercy. Inside the cabin, survivors crouched low, gripping the walls and fighting for any scrap of balance as the dizziness deepened with every lurch.
Roll's past thirty degrees! We keep taking these waves broadside, we're going over!
Starboard ten. Get the bow into it!
On the bridge, the red night navigation lights darkened every face to a shadow.
Compass, wind speed, pitch and roll, the instruments jumped wildly, and the roll indicator's needle swung again and again into glaring red.
The bow turned slowly to meet the charging wall of water.
A heartbeat later, the entire ship was lifted as if by a giant hand and then slammed down hard.
Cordelia stumbled and nearly fell, but threw herself over Karenina to shield her first.
No more! We lose any more speed, we lose steerage!
Cordelia gritted her teeth. At this speed, every second was a battle against the raw power of nature.
Another wave crashed over the bow, flooding the foredeck before pouring back out through the drains.
A hairline crack began to spread from an old weld at the ship's midsection.
The radio drowned in a storm of static.
We're off the plotted course! Cordelia!
Cordelia's eyes were fixed on the electronic chart.
Can we push the engines any harder? Larsen?
Cordelia! Water temperature ███. It's still climbing!
Across the electronic chart, an impossible warm zone burned in livid orange-red, swallowing the whole region.
The sea was warming, though winter held the calendar. That unsettling difference in temperature was spinning the wind into a fury that no prediction had accounted for.
And what came next was worse.
Cordelia, that cold front... It's that cold front.
Larsen shut his eyes, fear etched across his face, his voice trembling.
...It all aligned. Cordelia... the god has made the "perfect storm."
It rolled over the entire hull, the surge hammering the ship and scouring the empty deck.
The vessel heaved with each gasping breath of the sea, and for a terrifying moment, gravity inverted.
Fresh damage! Starboard side, midships, a crack in the outer plate!
One disaster followed another. Larsen's eyes went wide, and he murmured under his breath, barely keeping his panic at bay.
The ship never finished its inspection...
Do we have anyone free for damage control? Onni?
Cyclic stress has caused fatigue fracturing in the hull...
Forget that, Larsen! Watch the engine room!
Cordelia's sharp rebuke snapped Larsen out of his daze. The young engineer immediately began his checks.
Cordelia watched the ship's readings turn red one by one, her fists clenching tighter with every alert.
Everyone left on the bridge, get to the damaged sections now! We're out of spare hands.
The Karenin stays on the water. That's the only priority! Damage control...
Go where you're useful. You're better at damage control than most.
Not a trace of hesitation showed in the young woman's eyes.
The soldiers' footsteps soon faded beyond the bridge.
Countless windows flickered across the screens, and her palms were slick with sweat. Updates surged in faster than she could process them, but the only sound left on the bridge was her own breathing.
Cordelia's hands flew across the control console.
The helm, the telegraph, and the ballast valves, it was work meant for three, and now it all bore down on her shoulders.
She strapped Karenina tight against her chest to free her hands, and the baby simply stared, wide-eyed, at a world that tilted and swayed.
(Just a little longer... Get past the storm's edge. Just a little longer.)
Another wall of water bore down on them.
The Karenin clawed its way up the wave's face, then came crashing down.
The moment the hull slammed into the trough, a dull crack burst from somewhere deep inside the ship.
It was the sound of steel tearing apart.
Alarms drowned out everything as red lines crept across the control panel, spreading toward both sides of the hull at a pace too fast to ignore.
Cordelia, that's it! Pull back! Get out of there! Now!
Reef ahead!!! The ship's breaking apart and we can't steer! What do we do?!
This is Cordelia to all hands. Everyone in the living quarters, evacuate to the sonar control room at the stern! The ship is breaking apart!
I repeat: all personnel, fall back to the sonar control room at the stern. Don't stop for anything. Run!
She slammed the radio switch for the stern engine room.
Cordelia, get out of there! Head to the stern, now!
...You've lost your mind! Pull back! The ship is splitting apart!
Listen to me, Larsen! The power unit is at the stern, and it's barely damaged. That means...
...That means even with half a ship, our propulsion is still functional...
Cordelia gave a slight nod, her fingers already flying across the console.
Drop the main engine RPM. Keep just enough thrust to maintain headway, nothing more. We don't want to tear the damaged stern bearing.
Wait... that only gives us forward thrust. We'd have almost no way to correct lateral drift. The reef ahead...
I know. That's why I'm still here. I'm getting the hydraulics back up in the chain locker.
If we drop it, the drag will pull us off course. Just enough to clear the reef!
The keel is almost gone. I have to finish before it gives completely...
But the moment that anchor drops, the force will shear the bow clean off. You have to move fast—
She cast one last look at the hull readings.
(At this speed... I can still make it.)
The dull ache in her body had grown impossible to ignore, but she had left the mechanical plant behind at the lighthouse, and with it, the only relief she had.
Karenina stirred against her chest and let out a tiny, soft whimper.
Don't be scared, Karenina. We're going on a grand adventure.
Cordelia's eyes never left the control console. As the storm howled around her, her finger pressed down on the final key.
The hydraulic system in the anchor chain compartment rumbled back to life, and the progress bar began to inch forward.
The entire bridge sank into a heavy, oppressive darkness. Only the occasional pale gleam of a wave beyond the window broke through the black.
In that darkness, she gathered Karenina into the curve of her arm.
Sweetheart, we're going to run now.
She had to outrun the hydraulic system's progress bar. Outrun death itself.
Through the curtain of rain, the fracture at the bow tore open like a gaping abyss. Black seawater surged up through the split, wrenching the two halves of the deck farther and farther apart.
She was drenched through, and the deck tilted sharply beneath her, each step sinking as though the ground itself was collapsing.
Then a severed cable came whipping down through the air and slashed clean through the straps binding Karenina to Cordelia's back.
In that critical moment, Cordelia threw herself headlong into the path of the deadly steel cable and lunged forward, snatching the falling bundle before it could drop.
The child, a heartbeat from slipping away, was pulled back into her arms.
A white-hot rupture seemed to split her spine and shoulders, and the agony crushed the air from Cordelia's lungs before she could even cry out.
Through the curtains of rain, she strained to lift her gaze.
The fracture was still spreading. The bow was slowly slipping away from the rest of the hull.
The moment the anchor dropped, the force would tear the bow clean off and drag it beneath the waves.
On the stern deck, Larsen pushed against the tide of fleeing survivors and ran to the very edge of the fracture.
The young woman clutched the bundle tight against her chest, her face smeared with blood, and limped toward the widening gap.
Rope! Is there a rope?! Someone get a rope!
We don't have one long enough!
On the bridge, the anchor chain's progress bar hit zero.
A muffled thud shuddered through the entire hull.
The winch turned to its limit, and the last length of anchor chain slipped beneath the surface.
The anchor bit into the seabed, and the heavy chain followed link by link, settling onto the ocean floor.
The tension shot up through the taut anchor chain from the deep, and the ship's keel let out a piercing, overstressed wail before snapping apart with a thunderous roar.
The Karenin finally gave way, splitting in two as seawater surged through the breach.
Then, a series of tremors traveled up the anchor chain. The force still biting deep into the seabed wrenched the Karenin's stern and subtly shifted her course.
It was less than thirty degrees, but just enough for the hull to scrape past the reef by a hair.
Steel groaned as the bow tilted, moments from sinking.
The young woman stepped to the very edge of the fracture. The gap between the two halves had already widened beyond what anyone could cross.
On the other side, her companions waited in desperation.
****! There has to be a way! Think of something! Cordelia's still over there!
Cordelia looked down at Karenina, cradled in her arms.
The sea wind had chilled the baby's face to ice.
She took out the backup energy core. Its greatest purpose had vanished the moment she left the mechanical potted plant behind on the island.
But its thermal function was still just enough to keep a baby warm.
People always said being born into the Erhorn family was the greatest gift fate ever gave me.
Cordelia gently tucked the crystal into the folds of Karenina's swaddle.
Then I'm giving all my luck to you, Karenina.
Once more, she bundled the baby tight.
Because of my fault. Because of the selfishness of the people who love me. Because of the greed of my so-called family.
Because of all of it, you were thrown into a fate you never deserved.
She looked up at Larsen across the growing gap.
This is what I owe you... a life to be lived whole.
With the rain streaming down her face, she let a smile touch her lips.
Don't become whatever fate wants you to be, Karenina. Rage against it, always...
The girl brought by the Karenin... my Karenina.
She raised the child high above her head and drew back with everything she had left.
The sound of metal snapping cut through the storm.
It was the prosthesis in her spine and arms giving way.
The tiny bundle arced through the night sky. The crystal traced a line through the darkness like a falling star.
For a fleeting moment, Cordelia's mind went elsewhere. She should have kissed the child one last time.
Larsen threw himself forward, his body pitching over the edge of the fracture, heels nearly lifting off the deck. Lumi and Onni seized him from behind and held on with everything they had.
Three pairs of hands stretched wide into the storm.
Larsen dropped to his knees on the deck and clutched the warm bundle against his chest. He lifted his head and stared toward the gap.
With every last ounce of strength, she cried out one final plea.
Larsen! Whatever happens, protect her! Protect this ship! Don't you dare give up!!
Keep her running! Every minute you buy is another minute of hope!!!
A massive wave surged up through the fracture.
The wall of water crashed over the bow and swallowed everything whole.
When the wave finally receded, the other side of the fracture had vanished behind a shroud of rain-driven mist. There was nothing left to see.
Half an hour had passed since the break, and the stern was still tilting.
Survivors pressed together in tight clusters, their whispered prayers and sharp arguments filling every inch of the shrinking space.
...What do we do? ...Are we all going to die here?
...We're sinking... only half a ship left... we're finished...
A sickening metallic moan rose from the bulkhead while the sea forced its way through ruptured welds and surged into the stern's auxiliary engine room.
The auxiliary room is flooding... What now...?
Everyone out of there. Abandon the compartment.
Larsen. You need to make the call. Now.
Cordelia is gone. You're the only marine engineer we have left.
You're the only one who knows how to keep this half a ship running.
Rookie! Stop thinking so hard and just do what a marine engineer does!
...I can manage the heading through the engines. Keep us moving toward the target...
But we can't take on any more water. Otherwise, we'll never last until rescue.
Right. All the watertight doors in the main corridor need to be sealed.
How many soldiers still fit for duty?
We have no way to assess the actual damage. The compartments are flooding. Anyone who goes down there will be in serious—
We're soldiers. We have to be tougher than that.
Lumi was holding Karenina close. Away from Cordelia's arms, the baby had gone quiet again, still as a little doll.
Lumi cupped her tiny face, wiped the seawater from her cheeks, and lifted her eyes to Onni.
Stay with Larsen. F.O.S. only sent us two of you...
I'm graduating this year. And even though I haven't, I'm still a soldier.
F.O.S. doesn't train soldiers who run.
Lyndae swept her gaze across everyone gathered in the room and rose to her feet.
No more hesitation, Larsen. We need a plan, and we need orders.
...The flooding in the auxiliary room took out the voltage. The watertight doors won't close automatically.
We can't manually close all of them.
No. Someone has to go to the emergency power room and reset the breaker by hand.
Flip a breaker? Sounds easy enough for a medic.
Lumi looked at her, shaking her head with a smile.
After power is back, some doors still won't seal on their own. Those have to be closed manually.
I'll take a team and check every one.
There shouldn't be too many faulty watertight doors. If they pooled everyone they had left, they could cover them all.
But I'll need most of the people for this.
...We still need someone back on deck.
Out in the storm, amid the crashing waves, it was the most dangerous position of all.
Lumi drew a deep breath and stepped into the compartment where the survivors were sheltered.
Can you watch her for me?
The girl in the red dress lifted her head, her eyes hollow and unfocused, and stared at Lumi without expression.
When Uncle Larsen gets you out of here, give her to him.
You remember what Cordelia told you? Hold the baby.
The girl in the red dress took the tiny infant into her arms once more, and the void behind her gaze kindled with a fragile glimmer.
I'll hold her tight until you come back.
Lumi placed the spent energy core from Karenina's swaddle into Larsen's hands.
Their figures vanished through the doorway.
He already knew the answer, so he asked nothing.
Larsen returned to the control console and placed his trembling hands back on the keys.
He was the only one left now.
Water had flooded the main corridor to ankle depth, mercury-gray seawater seeping steadily through the fissures.
Onni and the others moved through the passage, checking each watertight door as the water climbed toward their knees.
Well, at least the circuits are intact. Otherwise, the second we stepped in here, we'd be—zzzt.
They came to a halt before a door that was badly warped.
...Frame's too bent. A jack won't cut it. We need power back, get the hydraulic pump on the other side running...
Then we push together from this end.
But... the latch on this side is broken. It won't seal.
This side's gone. The one down the corridor is still good.
The soldiers said nothing. Once they sealed the watertight door on the other side, they would be shut out in the corridor with it.
Just then, Lumi's voice crackled through the comms.
I'm at the emergency power room. Water's at the ankle.

In truth, the water had already risen past her knees. Murky seawater swirled with slicks of oil and floating debris. The distribution panels sat half-submerged, their electrical components already corroding.
At the main corridor entrance, Onni reached into his pocket without thinking and pulled out the cigarette Gunnar had left him, flicking his lighter.
Gunnar's last one. Given how things are... let me have this, little Lumi? Just this once?
From the other end of the line came the sound of her laughter.
She offered no protest this time.
Onni worked the lighter repeatedly, and each small flame sparked to life before the dark swallowed it back.
When did the damn thing get wet...

Inside the power room, Lumi crouched down. The water had already risen halfway up her thighs. Every indicator light on the distribution panels had gone dark. The only light came from the faint phosphorescent strip on the emergency breaker handle.
It was hovering just above the waterline.
Captain Onni, how's the door looking?
Little warped, no big thing. Soon as the power kicks in, it'll close... And once it does... we'll take a nice stroll back to the engine room.

Onni scratched the back of his head. The soldiers with him shared a quiet, wordless smile, then waded one by one toward the deeper water at the far side of the door. That was the only place from which the watertight door could be sealed.
Just a handle pull. Quick job.

The seawater had already risen past the terminals. The moment she reached in and threw the breaker, the high-voltage current would surge through the floodwater and complete a circuit straight through her body.
Captain Onni, you'd better run fast.
I don't want Lieutenant Lyndae laughing at you for finishing behind me.
Alright, alright. Time to flip the switch.
She said it lightly, almost bright.

In the main corridor, Onni and a few soldiers knelt half-submerged, the water up to their chests. Behind them, the others bore down on the base of the hydraulic jack, fighting to keep it from slipping under the pressure.
He turned his head to the side and wedged his shoulder against the door panel, legs bent, throwing his full weight into the direction of the push that would come the moment the current hit.
The damp cigarette tucked against his chest seemed to burn.
Lumi drew a deep breath, gripped the handle beneath the water with her right hand, and shoved it upward.
The arc flared like a lighter catching, a brief and brilliant spray of sparks.
Blue-white current shot through the conductive seawater and wrapped around the figure standing in it in an instant.
Lumi poured the last of her strength into her grip, along with every searing ounce of pain.
In the same moment, the heavy watertight door ground shut before Onni and the others.
The current still tore through her body as her consciousness slowly bled away into the freezing water.
Her strength ebbed, and the cold vanished. She could no longer feel it.
She collapsed into the seawater, choked on a few mouthfuls, and watched the bubbles drift upward in silence.
Lumi tilted her face toward the surface, where the fractured light above grew smaller and farther with each heartbeat.
That light looked just like the stars that shimmered across the domed ceiling of the academy hall.
(Guess I'm graduating... ahead of you... after all.)
The dark gathered her in with the tenderness of a held breath.
Death settled over her the way delicate fingers would press the ember from a cigarette, without hurry, without sound.
The door sealed shut. The water level in the main corridor near the engine room stopped rising, and Onni and the others could no longer turn back.
Job's done. Now it's on the rookie.
We'll wait a bit. Can't be worse than going days without a smoke.
Everyone laughed anyway, even though the joke was hardly funny.
The water kept climbing, from chest to neck, while the emergency lights near the ceiling flickered on and off.
For a long, long moment, there was no answer from the other end. Onni closed his eyes.
The seawater kept pouring in. No one knew how much time had passed, and no one spoke anymore.
In the dark, the only sound was the soft gurgle of water seeping through the cracks.
The world beyond the deck was shredding itself.
Lyndae balanced on the wreckage of the railing, her fingers locked around torn metal, blood welling in her palms. The storm hurled wind and water at her face, stealing her sight.
A voice broke through the radio static.
Flooding has stopped. The team got it done. But they're not answering.
It was meant to be good news, but the voice on the other end of the radio trembled with barely concealed panic. Lyndae let out a quiet laugh.
Rookie, when you think you can't hold on anymore, tell yourself, just hold on one more minute.
You're the marine engineer, and right now, you're also this ship's captain.
Her vision blurred. She could not tell if the red haze seeping into her sight was blood or something else.
But she saw it. The massive wave that swept everything before it, the Ragnarok that threatened to swallow the world.
She wanted to look back, even though turning would only show her the faltering lights. There were still people alive back there. The presence of life always lent a person immeasurable courage.
So she did not look back.
Swells above ten meters. Zero visibility. Reduce speed, head into the waves.
Nature's fury had shaped a wall of water that could never be crossed. She did not look away. She did not try to dodge.
Onni had always hated how insufferably arrogant she was.
That's a hell of a view.
The ocean stretched endlessly, and its waves raged with a terrible beauty that humbled the soul.
She planted herself and crashed into the towering surge.
Speed reduced. Heading into the waves.
Deck... report heading and confirm rudder response.
He had lost count of how many times he had spoken those words.
The black sea swallowed everything, and the hull tilted to its breaking point.
Another massive wave slammed into the ship.
Larsen was hurled against the console, and on pure instinct, he seized the control lever with a death grip.
Cordelia... what do I do now...
(One more minute... just one more minute...)
He shut his eyes tight, his breath coming in short, ragged bursts.
(Can I really do this... There's no way I can...)
It was an unstoppable doom, where Balder fell, and Odin lunged toward Death in rage...
He released the control lever and crumpled to the floor. Perhaps it was all right to give up now.
Here, the script of fate would turn to its last page.
Through the howl of the storm, another sound cut through.
Is anyone aboard? Can you hear me? This is a World Government rescue team! Is there anyone still alive in there?
A searchlight swept down from above, the rigging thrashing wildly in the wind.
Every survivor still breathing poured onto the deck.
The girl in the red dress clutched the baby tight against her chest.
Wind's too heavy! We can't hold position! Get on, fast as you can!
The rescuer's voice blasted through the loudspeaker, only to be ripped apart by the wind.
The survivors surged forward, the instinct to survive overriding everything else in that moment.
Her voice was too small, nearly swallowed by the rain, the shouting, and the roar of the helicopter blades.
Wedged in the crush of bodies, she stumbled and almost fell.
A hand shot out and gripped the red-dressed girl firmly by the shoulder, steadying her, then lifted her off her feet.
The tiny infant cradled in her arms drew every eye around them.
A hush swept through the noise for just a heartbeat. It was the orphan the soldiers had taken away.
Her golden eyes blinked calmly in the storm, utterly unaware of the chaos around her.
She had been so well cared for. Now, those who had cared for her were gone.
The first hand reached out and took the baby.
There's a child here! A baby!
Another pair of hands took her.
Not everyone realized what was happening.
But after that first hand reached out, a second followed, and then a third. Along that path of life, there was always another hand ready to receive the child.
Up front! Take the baby! Pass her up!
Aboard this final ark, every soul pushed forward, but every soul also turned and extended a hand.
Each hand moved with the crowd, driven by nothing but life's raw instinct.
The instinct called kindness, in the test of survival.
The hands that had fought for the ropes now formed the lifeline that carried the child forward.
The wind and waves still raged, but on that small stretch of deck, a strange stillness settled.
Cradled by countless hands, the tiny life wrapped in swaddling cloth made her slow way to the front of the line.
Through the chaos, a pair of hands reached down from the aircraft.
The girl in the red dress lifted her head for one last look at that tiny face.
The hands along the lifeline received the swaddle with steady care.
Infant on board! Hurry! Get her warm!
The rescue team member practically shouted the order into the communicator.
On the deck, every face tilted upward, watching her climb higher and higher until she vanished into the light.
Even as the storm continued to rage and the night heaved around them.
